summary: Defines a Telnet option that enables a binary data mode between the two Telnet modules. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet normally only sends plain text. The TRANSMIT-BINARY option lets the two ends agree to send raw 8-bit data instead, with a small rule to safely send the control byte itself.

questions: how to send binary data over telnet
what does iac iac mean in telnet
subtitle: An option that lets Telnet send and receive raw 8-bit data instead of only NVT ASCII text.

tldr.problem: Telnet normally carries text, but sometimes programs need to send arbitrary 8-bit data without switching to a higher-level protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The TRANSMIT-BINARY option (code 0) uses WILL/WON'T and DO/DON'T to negotiate binary mode for each direction separately, so characters are interpreted as 8-bit data. In binary mode, IAC IAC represents the data value 255.
tldr.outcome: When agreed, the connection carries binary data; a WON'T or DON'T reverts to NVT ASCII. The option is an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 856 is an Internet Standard with no known updates or obsoletes.

sections.title: Why Binary Transmission
sections.content: RFC 856 defines the TRANSMIT-BINARY option with code 0. It provides a way to have a binary path within Telnet without using a higher-level protocol such as FTP. The existing IAC mechanism in Telnet makes this a natural extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want to send data that isn't just text. This option gives Telnet a safe way to do that without moving to another program.

sections.title: Negotiating Binary Mode
sections.content:
The option is negotiated using four commands: IAC WILL TRANSMIT-BINARY (requests or confirms sending binary data), IAC WON'T TRANSMIT-BINARY, IAC DO TRANSMIT-BINARY (requests or confirms that the other side sends binary data), and IAC DON'T TRANSMIT-BINARY. A connection is in binary mode only when one side has requested it and the other has acknowledged it. The default is WON'T and DON'T (not binary).

If binary mode is already in effect, receiving WON'T or DON'T demands a return to standard NVT ASCII. If not in binary mode, they mean continue in the present mode.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks to switch to binary, the other agrees. Either side can ask to stop, which sends both back to plain text. The agreement applies separately to each direction of data flow.

sections.title: How Data Is Interpreted
sections.content: When binary mode is in effect, characters not preceded by IAC are interpreted as 8-bit binary data. The exception is IAC IAC, which represents the 8-bit data value 255. IAC followed by a real Telnet command remains a command; IAC followed by an undefined command has the same meaning as IAC NOP (though not normally sent).
sections.plainLanguage: In binary mode, almost everything is treated as raw data. To send the special control byte itself as data, you send it twice.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Binary mode must be negotiated separately for each direction. The loop-preventing rules of the Telnet protocol apply. Implementations may refuse other options (such as EBCDIC) while in binary mode, though combinations are possible if both hosts agree.

The rule for reverting: once binary mode is agreed, a WON'T or DON'T always reverts to NVT ASCII (not to the previous mode), to avoid needing a stack of transitions. Implementers must also consider whether terminals and processes can actually pass all 8-bit characters, as some systems intercept or convert certain characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Each direction needs its own agreement. Stopping binary mode always goes back to plain text, not to some other encoding. Not all systems can safely handle every possible 8-bit value.

cells: Sender requests or confirms it will send 8-bit binary data
If in binary mode, demands return to NVT ASCII; otherwise refuses
Requests or confirms the other side should send binary data
If in binary mode, demands return to NVT ASCII; otherwise demands current mode
